title: Mong Mao → Upper Myanmar → Patkai
text: Sukaphaa’s party is conventionally said to have left Mong Mao in 1215. The gold winding trail previews a reconstructed corridor through western Yunnan, the upper Irrawaddy near Waingmaw/Myitkyina, Mogaung and Hukawng toward Nong Yang and Pangsau. Bends are illustrative; intermediate stop dates and several old place identifications are unresolved. This is a migration route, not Ahom territory in Myanmar.

title: Across the Patkai to Namrup
text: Sukaphaa entered the Assam plains by an overland Patkai crossing. Pangsau is the conventional pass identification; the line shown is an approximate corridor. Namrup is the first Assam stop in this sequence. This is a migrating group, not yet the later Ahom kingdom.

title: Dihing exploration and Tipam
text: The chronicle sequence crosses the Sessa, goes upstream on the Dihing, then returns downstream to Tipam. Exact camps and the riverbank track cannot be recovered. The river excursion is schematic; no upstream camp is plotted as an exact site.

title: Mungklang / Abhaypur
text: Sukaphaa moved from Tipam to Mungklang Chekhru, identified in histories as Abhaypur. Its exact historical site is unresolved here, so it is listed without a false map pin. Earlier locality patches stand for the settlement network, not continuous possession.

title: Habung: cultivation and floods
text: The chronicles place a move down the Brahmaputra to Habung in 1240. Flooding prompted another move in 1244. The pin uses the modern Dhakuakhana-area identification; the historical tract was broader and is also associated with the Dhemaji region.

title: Downstream to Dikhoumukh, then Ligirigaon
text: From Habung the party followed the Brahmaputra downstream to the Dikhou mouth and travelled up the Dikhou toward Ligirigaon (Song-Tak), near present Nazira. Changing channels and uncertain old settlements make the trail a corridor rather than a literal boat track.

title: Simaluguri settlement
text: Simaluguri became the next base, with a detachment left at Ligirigaon. The historical settlement is associated with the modern Simaluguri vicinity; the marker is approximate. These are local footholds, not a continuous kingdom stretching to Sadiya.

title: Charaideo: capital and a small kingdom
text: Charaideo became the enduring capital in 1253 in the conventional chronology; some histories give 1251–1252. The surrounding foothill-and-plain core grew through coercion, accommodation and marriage with Moran and Barahi groups. The reconstructed core remains much smaller than the 16th-century realm.

title: Toward the Dikhou–Namdang tract
text: Suteuphaa’s reign is associated with gaining land from the Kacharis in the Dikhou–Namdang tract. The exact acquisition year is unknown: 1268 starts the display window, not a dated conquest. This small western addition precedes a long period of consolidation.

title: Consolidation, not continuous expansion
text: The kingdom largely held its Upper Assam core for roughly two centuries. Campaigns, a Kamata conflict and eastern diplomacy do not establish permanent annexation of the routes traversed. Sudangphaa’s Patkai settlement belongs to frontier consolidation, not an automatic conquest of all intervening hills.

title: Suhungmung: preparations for expansion
text: Suhungmung’s reign brought administrative reorganisation, a population enquiry in 1510 and campaigns against neighbouring groups. The map retains the inherited core until specific territorial acquisitions are reported.

title: Habung annexed
text: Habung was annexed under Suhungmung. A separate north-bank patch marks this gain; it does not yet colour the whole Chutia kingdom as Ahom.

title: Dikhoumukh fighting and eastern gains
text: A Chutia offensive was defeated at Dikhoumukh and on the river. Ahom gains around Mungkhrang and a Namdang locality followed. This eastern Namdang must not be confused automatically with the Sivasagar tributary of that name; the eastern patch is a broad Dihing-area locator, not an exact fort.

title: Chutia counterattack: eastern setback
text: The Chutias retook Mungkhrang and the associated eastern tract after the Ahom garrison withdrew. The eastern Ahom patch disappears and a contested Chutia recovery patch returns. Sources do not securely establish the extent of any Habung recovery, so the north-bank ownership is shown as unresolved during this interval.

title: Ahom recovery and advance
text: Suhungmung recovered the lost eastern tract and established a fort farther east in the river-mouth zone. The source names Sessa and Tiphao; modern identifications vary. The expansion is schematic and is not labelled as a securely located fort.

title: Sadiya and the Chutia kingdom annexed
text: The decisive campaigns ended the independent Chutia monarchy in 1523–1524. Sadiya came under an Ahom governor, the Sadiya Khowa Gohain. The eastern domain now joins the older core; this does not yet imply the later western extent toward the Kolong.

title: Westward campaigns against the Kacharis
text: Ahom power advanced in the Dhansiri region through successive campaigns; Dimapur was sacked in 1536. The broad western map phase begins in 1532 as an approximate campaign-stage anchor. The 1537 map then shows the later Kolong-side expansion.

date: Before the late 14th century · founding date uncertain
title: Sadiya centre; early extent unknown
text: 1187 and Birpal belong to a later founding tradition, not a securely dated conquest sequence. Only a small symbolic Sadiya-area patch is shown in this early window. It neither measures the early state nor assigns the later Lakhimpur–Dhemaji domain to it.

title: Chutia power becomes clearer in the records
text: Chronicles place conflict with the Ahoms in Sutuphaa’s time, conventionally around 1376. Nandin / Nandisvara is the earliest king remembered in the inscription genealogy of Satyanarayana. This supports an eastern political centre, not a precise founding year or frontier.

title: Dhenukhana grant: western evidence appears
text: The grant of Satyanarayana and Pratyakshanarayana provides dated evidence in the Habung–Dhakuakhana region. An additional locality patch marks this evidence. Its appearance in 1392 is an attestation date, not proof that the tract was conquered that year.

title: Ghilamara: Lakshminarayana’s grant
text: Lakshminarayana’s Ghilamara charter adds another dated western record. Its locality patch joins the earlier Sadiya and Habung-region symbols. The map does not fill the intervening country from this grant alone or assign a conquest to 1401.

title: Sadiya–Chepakhowa charter and Habung
text: Durlabhnarayana’s charter names a Habung authority. Genealogical references to a Kamatapura ruler have competing interpretations and do not justify colouring all Kamata as Chutia territory. The Habung and Sadiya markers locate regions, not the charter’s exact original issue/find sites.

title: Tamreswari: an eastern royal inscription
text: The Paya–Tamreswari inscription records Mukta-dharmanarayana’s temple enclosure wall in 1442. Alongside the earlier grants, this supports a mid-15th-century domain context in the eastern plains and river valleys. The wider envelope is reconstructed, not a conquest in 1442; upland Arunachal is not automatically annexed.

title: Habung lost; Ahom–Chutia war
text: Ahom annexation of Habung was followed by Chutia offensives and reverses in the Dihing–Dikhoumukh theatre. The Habung patch changes owner separately from the Sadiya heartland. Dhirnarayana’s exact accession is unknown, and royal names vary between chronicles.

title: Mungkhrang recovered
text: A Chutia counterattack recovered the eastern tract around Mungkhrang. The map restores a symbolic recovery patch there. Claims of a simultaneous, complete reconquest of Habung are less secure and are not treated as a settled border change.

title: Ahom counteroffensive
text: The Ahoms recovered their eastern losses and advanced toward the river mouths. Chutia control contracted toward Sadiya before the final campaign. A land grant or findspot by itself cannot define every wartime frontier.

title: Independent monarchy ends; people and traditions continue
text: Ahom annexation ended independent Chutia kingship around 1523–1524. Chronicles disagree over the last royal names and deaths. Chutia communities, specialists and Deori religious traditions continued; a polity’s disappearance from the map does not mean its population disappeared.

title: Sandhya’s western reorganisation
text: The map begins with a Kamatapur–western plains focus and an uncertain successor region farther east. This is a change of political centre, not a newly conquered kingdom growing from zero. The capital-shift date and frontier are approximate.

title: Rival rulers and competing authority
text: Durlabhnarayana and Indranarayana belong to approximate 14th-century chronologies. Kamata authority was contested; the eastern reach is dashed and separate from the western core. No automatic, continuous rule to the later Barnadi limit is assumed.

title: Fragmentation before the Khen
text: Arimatta and successor traditions cannot furnish exact borders or reigns. The reconstruction contracts to the western Kamata focus, while independent Bhuyan localities remain distinct. The c.1365 division is a display anchor, not a securely dated territorial collapse.

title: Niladhwaj: Kamatapur base
text: A western core represents the early Khen kingdom. The c.1440 foundation is conventional; the later Nilambar footprint is not shown at the dynasty’s beginning.

title: Chakradhwaj: consolidation
text: An intermediate western-plains envelope locates the kingdom during consolidation. The larger outline is a schematic stage, not a dated annexation of each district.

title: Nilambar: wider Kamata domain
text: Nilambar’s later kingdom reached farther into lower Assam; a broad reconstruction extends toward the Barnadi area. The transition at 1480 follows approximate reign chronology. Husain Shah captured Kamatapur in 1498.

title: Regional chiefs, not a single Bhuyan kingdom
text: Bhuyan is a category of landed chiefs, not one dynasty or a permanently united set of twelve. A few open locality patches indicate a central-valley setting only. Dates, membership and boundaries are uncertain; this early interval does not establish the later Chandivara lineage at these precise sites.

title: Chandivara and the Barnadi region
text: Charit traditions associate Chandivara’s group with Langamaguri / Lengamaguri near the Barnadi. Exact date and site are unresolved. A north-Guwahati/Barnadi-area patch is a regional locator, while separate central-valley chiefs retain their own localities.

title: Bardowa: the Shiromani Bhuyan lineage
text: Sankardeva was born into a Bhuyan family at Bardowa in 1449. This adds a securely associated south-bank centre; it is not the year the Bhuyans conquered Bardowa. The patches represent distinct seats, not a unified country across both banks.

title: Sultanate pressure and local resistance
text: The Bengal conquest displaced the Khen monarchy. The extent and duration of the garrisons varied; local chiefs remained important. The western resistance stage is separated from the older central-valley seats.

title: Local recovery after Bengal’s withdrawal
text: Independent chiefs re-emerged after the Bengal garrisons lost control. The c.1505 change is an approximate display anchor, not proof of a single Harupnarayan state extending from Sankosh to Subansiri.

title: Koch advance in the west; Ahom pressure in the east
text: Biswa Singha subdued western chiefs over a sequence of campaigns, while Ahom expansion reduced eastern autonomy. The patches contract in stages; neither all chiefs nor both banks fell in one year.

title: Chiefly independence declines; offices persist
text: Regional Bhuyan seats were progressively subordinated by larger states. This map ends the independent-locality layer in the 1530s, not every Bhuyan family or office. Local and district histories also record later Bhuyan authority and resistance.
